Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis traditionally assigned to Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QGenb in DJD XII (Davila). Its editor suspected it may instead derive from Wadi Murabba'at: its leather is coarse and poorly prepared, unusual for Qumran, its script is typologically late, and no fragment of it was identified among photographs from the controlled Cave 4 excavations. Its best-preserved portion is a relatively intact column covering the opening of Genesis 1 (Genesis 1:1-25a in the Lyon summary), with further scattered remains from Genesis 2, 4 and 5. The surviving text is essentially identical to the Masoretic Text; one exhibit summary notes a single minor spelling difference in Genesis 1:15.
Significance: An early witness to the stability of the Genesis text: a copy made around the turn of the era already agrees with the Masoretic Text that underlies modern Hebrew Bibles, including at the creation account in Genesis 1. Its value is as a textual witness, not as a complete Genesis scroll — only scattered verses survive, so it proves nothing about chapters it does not preserve.

Description: A lengthy Hebrew copy of Exodus in palaeo-Hebrew script, published in DJD IX (Skehan, Ulrich, Sanderson). The original scroll occupied about 45 columns, spanning Exodus 6:25 to 37:16. It is poorly preserved in detail — no column survives entirely undamaged and many columns are represented only by scattered fragments — but its overall range and word-count (over 1,000 words preserved) make it the most extensive Exodus manuscript from Qumran.
Significance: The key witness to the expansive, pre-Samaritan form of Exodus: it attests harmonistic expansions similar to those in the Samaritan Pentateuch, showing that an expanded Exodus text circulated in the late Second Temple period alongside the shorter tradition that became the Masoretic Text. It therefore proves textual plurality in this period, not a single uniform Exodus text.

DateApprox: c. late 2nd century BC - 1st century AD (dating debated)
Description: A Hebrew Leviticus scroll in palaeo-Hebrew script, discovered in Cave 11 in January 1956 and held first at the Rockefeller Museum, where it was photographed in 1956 and again in detail by the Israel Antiquities Authority in 1970. It survives as the lower portion of its final columns, on parchment (kid leather, about 100 cm long as preserved), plus eighteen small fragments from earlier chapters. The main sheet covers Leviticus 22-27; the fragments extend coverage to Leviticus 4, 10, 11, 13-17 and 18-22. A single experienced scribe wrote it, with dots as word-dividers and letters suspended from ruled lines.
ImageCredit: Shai Halevi on behalf of the Israel Antiquities Authority — CC BY-SA 4.0
Significance: The most substantial Leviticus manuscript from Qumran and a showcase for the ancient palaeo-Hebrew script, the script formerly used for Torah scrolls in pre-exilic Israel. It is considered a primary witness to the proto-Masoretic text of Leviticus, making it a central witness for Leviticus textual history and for the laws of sacrifice, atonement, festivals and holiness in Leviticus 22-27.

Description: A lengthy Hebrew copy of Numbers from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XII (Jastram). Remains of 27 columns survive, covering Numbers 11-36 in fragments, written in early Herodian semiformal Hebrew script. A few lines are written in red ink. It is one of only a handful of Qumran biblical manuscripts with over 1,000 words preserved.
Significance: The fullest Numbers witness from Qumran, and a pre-Samaritan (expansionist) text: many of its variants agree with the Samaritan Pentateuch against the Masoretic Text, demonstrating that differing versions of Numbers circulated in the Second Temple period.

Description: A small but exceptionally well-preserved parchment manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, published by Sidnie White Crawford (JBL 109/2, 1990) as the All Souls Deuteronomy. It consists of two sheets and six columns — four complete columns and two partially damaged — with columns 2-6 on one continuous sheet of parchment. In the manuscript the passages appear in the order Deuteronomy 8:5-10, then Deuteronomy 5:1-6:1, an ordering that, with the blank space at the bottom of column 1, is the main reason scholars argue it is an excerpted/liturgical collection rather than a regular Deuteronomy scroll (an alternative explanation is incorrect repair of the scroll). Its script is unusually tiny, with waw and yod almost indistinguishable, and its orthography is much fuller than that of either the Masoretic Text or the Samaritan Pentateuch.
Significance: Crawford calls it the best-preserved of all the Deuteronomy manuscripts from Cave 4, and it preserves the Decalogue (Deuteronomy 5) in full. Its Decalogue generally follows Deuteronomy but is harmonised toward the Exodus parallel, including one variant unique to this manuscript: the addition of the Exodus reason for the Sabbath commandment. Press reports have called it the oldest complete copy of the Ten Commandments; that title is disputed — the Nash Papyrus (c. 150-100 BC) is older, and 4Q41 itself may be a liturgical excerpt rather than a Torah scroll — so the entry does not repeat the press claim as fact.

Description: Fragments of Joshua from Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QJosha (DJD 14). The surviving text spans five chapters (5, 6, 7, 8, 10), including the fall of Jericho material (chapter 6), the Achan episode (chapter 7), and the southern campaign (chapter 10). The Leon Levy record shows 44 images of this manuscript.
Significance: The fullest Qumran witness to Joshua. Its most discussed feature is the position of Joshua 8:34–35 before 5:2, showing that the blessings-and-curses passage circulated in a different place in the book; Ulrich cautions that it is not certain the altar-building verses (8:30–31) preceded them, since that text would fall in an unpreserved part of the preceding column. Its text shows variations in wording and omissions against the Masoretic Text, with some readings aligning with the Greek text.

Description: Fragments of Judges from Qumran Cave 1, published as 1QJudg (DJD 1, pp. 62-64, Barthelemy 1955). The surviving text covers parts of chapters 6, 8 and 9, including the Gideon and Abimelech material. The Leon Levy record lists Site Qumran Cave 1, Manuscript Type Biblical Compositions, Composition Type Scripture, Language Hebrew, Script Square, Period Hellenistic-Roman, Material Parchment, and 4 images. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.
Significance: One of three Qumran copies of Judges (with 4QJudga, covering chapter 6, and 4QJudgb, covering chapters 19 and 21), and the fullest of the three. Its text is close to the Masoretic Text. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.

Description: Fragments of Ruth from Qumran Cave 2, published as 2QRutha. The surviving text spans three chapters (2, 3 and 4): Ruth's gleaning and her meeting with Boaz (chapter 2), the threshing-floor scene (chapter 3), and the redemption transaction at the gate (chapter 4). The Leon Levy record shows 38 images of this manuscript. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.
Significance: The fullest Qumran witness to Ruth by chapter span and coverage (chapters 2–4). Ruth copies at Qumran show only slight variations from the Masoretic Text. The earlier Hasmonean copy 4Q104 preserves the continuous opening of the book (Ruth 1:1–12), and 4Q105 preserves Ruth 1:1–6, 12–15.

Description: The most extensive Samuel scroll from Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QSama (DJD 17, pp. 1-216, 217). In antiquity Samuel was one work, so this single scroll counts once and covers both 1 and 2 Samuel. It survives in 11 partially preserved columns and some 165 fragments with identified contents plus unidentified fragments, at 47 lines per column and about 32.7 cm high including the bottom margin. Only 8 scribal corrections are reported; the scroll was worn in antiquity and reinforced with papyrus pieces glued on the back plus 2 leather patches. The Leon Levy record lists Material Parchment, Script Square, Period Hellenistic-Roman, and 726 images.
Significance: The most important Qumran witness to Samuel. Many of its readings differ from the Masoretic Text but agree with the Septuagint / Old Greek. Its most famous contribution is the longer Nahash paragraph before 1 Samuel 11:1, attested by 4QSama — where the scribe first skipped part of it by homoioteleuton and then inserted the missing words between the lines — and by Josephus, Antiquities 6.68–71; the paragraph is absent from the Masoretic Text. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.

Description: A papyrus scroll of Kings from Qumran Cave 6, published as 6QpapKgs (DJD 3). In antiquity Kings was one work, so this single scroll counts once and covers both 1 and 2 Kings. It is poorly preserved on 94 papyrus fragments, of which only 17 have been identified. Its script is described as archaic, written in a less professional manner but with few errors. The Leon Levy record shows 170 images of this manuscript. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation.
Significance: The only one of the three Qumran Kings manuscripts that covers both 1 and 2 Kings (4Q54 and 5Q2 preserve 1 Kings only), and the fullest by coverage. It carries multiple literary variants, some found in other textual witnesses; Tigchelaar notes it was written in a less professional manner but with few errors, while 4Q54 was a nonprofessional copy on substandard material.

Description: The only identified Qumran copy of Chronicles, from Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QChr / 4QChron. It is a single fragment with letters from two columns, the first column unidentified and the second offering a few letters from four verses (2 Chronicles 28:27-29:3) — the death of Ahaz and the accession of Hezekiah. In antiquity Chronicles was one work, but only 2 Chronicles text survives in this manuscript, so Work and RelatedBooks list 2 Chronicles only.
Significance: The sole Qumran witness to Chronicles, and therefore the best-preserved by default. No 1 Chronicles passage survives at Qumran in any identified manuscript. Its surviving text is consistent with the Masoretic Text tradition. It is a Hebrew original, not a translation. Only a few letters survive from each of the four verses, so the identification rests on a small amount of text.

Description: The only identified Qumran copy of the Ezra-Nehemiah work, from Qumran Cave 4, published as 4QEzra (DJD 16, pp. 291-93, pl. 38). Three fragments preserve bits and pieces of Ezra chapters 4, 5 and 6, including the Aramaic section of Ezra (Ezra 4:9-6:5 is in Aramaic in the biblical text itself, and is preserved here in Aramaic — this is the original language of that passage, not a translation). In antiquity Ezra-Nehemiah was one work, and the DJD list labels this manuscript '4QEzra (= Ezra-Nehemiah)'; that label is about the ancient combined work, NOT evidence that Nehemiah text survives in it. Work and RelatedBooks therefore list Ezra only.
Significance: The sole Qumran witness to the Ezra-Nehemiah work, and therefore the best-preserved by default. Its surviving text is consistent with the Masoretic Text tradition. No Nehemiah verse text survives in any identified Qumran manuscript, so Nehemiah has no entry of its own; an earlier reported Nehemiah fragment was challenged as a forgery.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Job from Qumran Cave 4, written in Hasmonean script on thin, well-prepared skin, arranged stichometrically in narrow columns. Only a few fragments survive; editors estimate that a complete copy of Job in this format would have run to about 72 columns. It is one of six Job manuscripts from Qumran (2Q15, 4Q99, 4Q100, 4Q101, 4Q157, 11Q10), and the only Hebrew copy with more than small fragments preserved.
Significance: One of the oldest textual witnesses to the Hebrew book of Job, which reached its final redaction in the 3rd century BC. Its value is as an early Hebrew witness to the text of Job's speeches and Elihu's speeches (chapters 31-37) centuries before the medieval Masoretic manuscripts; its fragmentary condition means it cannot settle the book's textual history on its own, and its few corrections away from the Masoretic Text are noted rather than treated as a separate edition.

Description: The most substantial and best-preserved Psalms manuscript among the Dead Sea Scrolls: five sheets of leather still sewn together, about 4.25 metres long in its surviving body (28 columns, plus separate fragments A-F), discovered in Cave 11 in February 1956 and first unrolled in 1961. It contains 49 compositions. It is not a copy of the whole Psalter: it runs chiefly through Psalms 101-150, in an order different from the Masoretic Psalter, and it mixes canonical psalms with compositions not in the Masoretic Psalter.
PreservedPassages: Chiefly Psalms 101-150 in a non-Masoretic order (with gaps), plus Psalm 93, Psalm 151, Syriac Psalms 154-155, Sirach 51, the Plea for Deliverance, the Hymn to the Creator, the Apostrophe to Zion, David's Compositions, and David's Last Words (2 Samuel 23:7)
Significance: Shows that in the 1st century AD the order and contents of the later part of the Psalter were not yet fixed: 11Q5 arranges Psalms 101-150 differently from the Masoretic Text and adds psalms known from the Syriac tradition (151, 154, 155), Sirach 51, and previously unknown hymns, alongside a prose passage crediting David with 4,050 compositions. At the same time it confirms that most of these psalms were already circulating in Hebrew long before the medieval manuscripts, and its strong Davidic emphasis fits the Qumran community's messianic hopes. It is a liturgical collection, not a straight copy of the Masoretic Psalter, and must not be presented as one.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Proverbs from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script. It is the largest Qumran Proverbs copy: the published statistical count gives it about 126 words against about 42 for 4Q102 (4QProva, Proverbs 1:27-33; 2:1). The surviving verses come from the collections of individual proverbs in chapters 13-15, with two further verses from chapter 7 whose identification is marked uncertain in the published list.
Significance: An early Hebrew witness to Proverbs, about a thousand years older than the medieval Masoretic manuscripts. The surviving text stands close to the Masoretic Text, with only minor variation in the published count, so its chief value is confirming the early stability of these proverb collections rather than revealing a different edition of the book.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Ecclesiastes (Qohelet) from Qumran Cave 4, among the oldest Dead Sea Scrolls found at Qumran. The surviving text covers parts of chapters 5-7, including the well-known saying that sorrow is better than laughter (Ecclesiastes 7). It is the larger of the two Qumran Ecclesiastes copies: the published count gives it about 125 words against about 21 for 4Q110 (4QQohb, Ecclesiastes 1:10-15).
ImageCredit: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin — CC BY-SA 4.0
Significance: Pushes the Hebrew text of Ecclesiastes back to the mid-2nd century BC, centuries before the medieval manuscripts, and shows the book already in circulation in essentially its familiar form. Its variants against the Masoretic Text are minor in character; its importance is its age and its confirmation of the book's early transmission, not a rival text of Ecclesiastes.

Description: Three fragments (four columns) of a Hebrew copy of the Song of Solomon from Qumran Cave 4, in early Herodian script. The copy is selective: it omits Song of Solomon 3:6-8 and 4:4-7 and ends at 5:1, so it is an excerpted or anthologised copy rather than a complete book scroll. Scholars have debated its use: Emmanuel Tov at one point argued it was a liturgical text, later revised that to a text for private use, and then abstained from identifying its use, a position other scholars have also reached.
Significance: One of only four Qumran copies of the Song (4Q106, 4Q107, 4Q108, 6Q6), together preserving about 47 of the book's 117 verses. It confirms the Song was already being copied in Hebrew around the turn of the era, while its omissions and its ending at 5:1 show that at least one Qumran copy circulated the Song in a selective form. Small differences from the Masoretic Text, including word order, are preserved in its fragments.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Lamentations from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script, dated c. 30-1 BC. It preserves the opening chapter of Lamentations (chapter 1, with the pe/ayin verses in swapped order, 17 before 16, in the published contents) and one verse of chapter 2. It is one of four Lamentations manuscripts from Qumran (3Q3, 4Q111, 5Q6, 5Q7).
Significance: The fullest Lamentations witness at Qumran by published word count (about 193 words, against about 141 for 5Q6). It is also the most variant of the Qumran Lamentations copies against the Masoretic Text: in the published statistical count it shows 37 variants, and recent study argues that most of its differences are deliberate scribal creations rather than simple copying errors. It therefore shows the text of Lamentations still fluid in the 1st century BC, even though the great stability of most of the Masoretic tradition is also visible across the Qumran copies as a group.

CurrentLocation: Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Shrine of the Book)
Description: One of the seven scrolls first found in Qumran Cave 1 in 1947. Written on 17 sheets of stitched parchment, about 734 cm (24 feet) long, in 54 columns. It contains the whole Book of Isaiah in the order familiar from modern Bibles, apart from a few small damaged portions. Palaeography places the handwriting at about 150-125 BC (Tov); radiocarbon results also fall before the time of Jesus, and c. 125 BC is the round figure usually given.
Significance: The only Qumran biblical scroll preserved almost in its entirety, and the oldest known complete copy of Isaiah, roughly 1,000 years older than the medieval Masoretic manuscripts known before 1947. It agrees overwhelmingly with the Masoretic Text: the differences, numbering in the thousands, are mostly spelling and grammar, with only a small number affecting the sense of a line. It therefore shows both careful transmission over a millennium and that ancient copying was done by human scribes.

Description: The longest surviving copy of Jeremiah from Qumran, published in DJD XV (E. Tov, 'Jeremiah', in Qumran Cave 4, X: The Prophets, 1997, pp. 145-207, covering 4Q70, 4Q71, 4Q72, 4Q72a, 4Q72b). It survives only as fragments, but they span chapters 4 to 33, including the cup-of-wrath passage in chapter 25 and the restoration chapters 30-31. It is a proto-Masoretic copy: it follows the longer Masoretic order and text.
Significance: Together with 4QJera it proves that the longer Masoretic form of Jeremiah already existed in Hebrew in the Second Temple period. The shorter form behind the Greek Septuagint (about one-seventh shorter, with the oracles against the nations in a different place) is separately attested in Hebrew by 4QJerb and 4QJerd. Both editions therefore circulated in Hebrew side by side at Qumran; the difference is a real textual history, not a later Greek trimming of the Hebrew.

Description: The broadest surviving copy of Ezekiel from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (J. E. Sanderson, 'Ezekiel', in Qumran Cave 4, X: The Prophets, 1997, pp. 209-220; 4Q73 at pp. 209-214, against 4Q74 at pp. 215-218 and 4Q75 at pp. 219-220). It survives as fragments from four separated passages: chapters 10, 11, 23, and 41 - the temple vision (chapters 10-11), the parable of Oholibah (chapter 23), and the temple measurements (chapter 41). The DJD editor Sanderson describes its hand as late Hasmonaean, while the Cave 4 list gives it as Herodian.
Significance: A proto-Masoretic witness that agrees substantially with the Masoretic Text of Ezekiel, including in the temple-vision and temple-measurement passages. Its value is as an early, pre-Christian Hebrew witness to the text of Ezekiel: it shows the book circulating in essentially the form later preserved in the Masoretic tradition, well before the medieval codices.

Description: Described in the BASOR preliminary edition as 'the most extensively preserved scroll' of Daniel from Qumran (Ulrich, Part 1; 4QDanb and 4QDanc, the other two substantially preserved Cave 4 copies, followed as Part 2). It survives as fragments spanning Daniel 1 to 11. The preserved text follows the book's own language pattern: Hebrew in chapter 1 and from chapter 8 onward, Aramaic in the middle section (the preserved Aramaic portion runs from Daniel 2:9 through 7:28 in this copy). Portions within the ranges listed are incomplete; this is a fragmentary scroll, not a continuous text.
Significance: The widest single Qumran witness to Daniel, and the clearest single-copy proof that Daniel's Hebrew-Aramaic-Hebrew structure already existed in a first-century BC Hebrew/Aramaic copy. It agrees in substance with the Masoretic Text. It is NOT the oldest Daniel copy (that distinction belongs to 4QDanc, 4Q114, late 2nd century BC, preserving Daniel 10-11); its claim is extent, not age. Across all eight Qumran Daniel manuscripts every chapter except Daniel 12 is represented; Daniel 12:10 is quoted as Scripture in the Florilegium (4Q174), so the absence of chapter 12 from the surviving Daniel fragments is not evidence the book lacked it at Qumran.

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Hosea, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum (and, questionably, Habakkuk). The most extensive Qumran manuscript of the Twelve Minor Prophets: a single Hebrew scroll, originally containing the whole Twelve collection, now surviving in many fragments. Only about 916 words can still be attributed to biblical text. The scribe copied carefully in an early Herodian book hand from the last third of the 1st century BC and corrected himself in nine cases. It does NOT contain Haggai or Malachi in its surviving portions. Note: a possible Habakkuk 2:4 fragment in this scroll is identified only with a question mark in the scholarly summary and is not counted here as a Habakkuk copy.
RelatedBooks: Hosea; Joel; Amos; Obadiah; Jonah; Micah; Nahum; Zephaniah; Zechariah
Significance: Textually important against the Masoretic Text: not counting reconstructed variants, 69 cases of variation between the Masoretic Text, the Septuagint and 4QXIIg are preserved; 4QXIIg agrees with the Masoretic Text 15 times and against it 54 times (44 clear readings, a 4.80% deviation among 916 identifiable words), and also attests 39 non-aligned readings. Its orthography is slightly more plene than the Masoretic Text and uses some Qumran spellings. For Hosea, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah and Nahum it is the best-preserved Qumran biblical copy; for Habakkuk it is only a questionable single-verse fragment (see Description).
Work: Hosea; Joel; Amos; Obadiah; Jonah; Micah; Nahum; Zephaniah; Zechariah

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Joel only. A Hebrew Twelve Prophets scroll from Qumran Cave 4, surviving in fragments. Its surviving portions cover Hosea, Joel, Amos, Zephaniah and a questionable Malachi fragment. One summary describes it as containing many scribal mistakes but also very many original readings. Note: a possible Malachi 3:6-7 fragment in this scroll is identified only with a question mark and is not counted here as a Malachi copy. A possible Amos 1:1 fragment is likewise identified only with a question mark and is not counted here.
Significance: Best-preserved Qumran biblical copy of Joel: its Joel coverage (Joel 1:10-20; 2:1, 8-23; 3:6, 8-10, 12-19, 21 in English numbering) is substantially larger than 4Q82's Joel coverage. It also preserves a large block of Hosea 4 and Amos 3 and 7, useful for checking the Masoretic Text, but it is not best for Hosea or Amos (both: 4Q82) or Zephaniah (4Q77) or Malachi (4Q76).

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Zephaniah and Haggai. A Hebrew Twelve Prophets scroll from Qumran Cave 4, dated 150-125 BC, surviving in fragments. Its largest fragment preserves the bottom edge of the manuscript, which helps determine the manuscript's dimensions and reconstruct it. It shows the Twelve Prophets written as one continuous book at Qumran.
Significance: Best-preserved Qumran biblical copy of Zephaniah (Zephaniah 1:1-2; 2:13-15; 3:19-20) and of Haggai (Haggai 1:1-2; 2:2-4, five verses, against 4Q80's four Haggai verses, and the older of the two Haggai copies). Zephaniah's themes of judgment and redemption and Haggai's call to rebuild the temple after 586 BC are both present in this early copy.

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Zechariah only. A Hebrew Twelve Prophets scroll from Qumran Cave 4, dated 75-50 BC, surviving in fragments. Its surviving portions are almost exclusively from Zechariah, with a short Haggai section at the end of Haggai 2.
Significance: Best-preserved Qumran biblical copy of Zechariah: it preserves parts of Zechariah 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 12, far more than 4Q76 (Zechariah 14:18 only) or 4Q82 (Zechariah 10-12 fragments). Its text is described as of a textual type related to the Septuagint. For Haggai it is the runner-up, not the best: Haggai 2:18-21 (four verses) against 4Q77's Haggai 1:1-2; 2:2-4 (five verses).

Description: Best-preserved Qumran copy for Malachi only. A Hebrew Twelve Prophets manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, dated c. 150-125 BC (semicursive hand, c. 150-100 BC in one palaeographic discussion; described as pre-Qumranic, c. 150 BC, in a 2015 study). It preserves a substantial Malachi section (Malachi 2:10 to the end of the book), a single Zechariah verse, and Jonah fragments as published in DJD XV. Note: Jonah fragments once attributed to this scroll in DJD XV are disputed by a later study, which argues the composition following Malachi was in all likelihood not Jonah; they are not counted here as a Jonah copy. The Zechariah attribution itself rests on a few letters on a single small fragment and has been questioned (the letters could also come from Jonah 4:10-11).
Significance: Best-preserved Qumran biblical copy of Malachi by a wide margin: Malachi 2:10-4:6 (English numbering) survives here, including the closing Elijah passage (Malachi 4:5-6, Hebrew 3:23-24), against only a questionable Malachi 3:6-7 fragment in 4Q78. It is also important for the history of the Twelve as a collection: a 2015 study argues it probably contained only three or four of the shortest books, not all twelve, and that Malachi was followed by another composition that was in all likelihood NOT Jonah — so Malachi was not always the last book in a Twelve scroll, and the Twelve could be copied in sets as well as as a single collection.

Description: Seven fragments from Cave 1, published by Barthelemy in DJD I, preserving scraps from 1 Samuel 18 (Saul offering Merab to David) and from three passages in 2 Samuel (the pursuit of Sheba, the fight with the Philistine giants, and David's mighty men). One summary gives the giants passage as 2 Samuel 21:16-19 rather than 21:16-18; the range here follows the DJD-based Samuel survey. It is the only Samuel copy from Cave 1; the other three Qumran Samuel copies are all from Cave 4.
Significance: Shows Samuel was read at Qumran beyond Cave 4, and its variants include a missing long stretch in 2 Samuel 20:8 and distinctive readings of proper names, so it is an independent textual witness, not a copy of the other Samuel scrolls.

Description: Two fragments from Cave 2, published by Baillet in DJD III, of which one fragment is unidentified, preserving the end of Ruth 3: Boaz's promise to act as kinsman-redeemer, the gift of barley, and Naomi's advice to wait (Ruth 3:13-18). It is the second Cave 2 Ruth copy, distinct from the Batch 1 copy 2Q16 (2QRutha).
Significance: One of four Qumran copies of Ruth, all showing only slight variation from the Masoretic Text, so it adds to the evidence that the short book of Ruth was stably transmitted in the late Second Temple period.

Description: Three fragments from Cave 4, including the beginning of the book: the famine, Elimelech's family in Moab, the deaths of Elimelech, Mahlon and Chilion, and Naomi setting out to return to Judah with her daughters-in-law (Ruth 1:1-12). It is the first Cave 4 Ruth copy.
Significance: The earliest-opening witness to Ruth at Qumran, preserving the book's first verses, which no other Qumran Ruth copy preserves; like the other Ruth copies it agrees closely with the Masoretic Text.

Description: Three minute fragments from Cave 4, preserving parts of Ruth 1: the opening verses and Naomi's farewell to Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:1-6, 12-15). It is the second Cave 4 Ruth copy, distinct from 4Q104, and overlaps it only at the book's opening.
Significance: Completes the set of four Qumran Ruth copies (2Q16, 2Q17, 4Q104, 4Q105). Its Herodian date shows Ruth was still being copied at Qumran in the decades before the settlement's destruction.

Description: The second, fragmentary copy of Joshua from Qumran Cave 4, distinct from the Batch 1 copy 4Q47 (4QJosha). It preserves scraps from the crossing of the Jordan (Joshua 2-4) and from the allotment of land to Manasseh (Joshua 17). Verse-edge summaries differ slightly between editions: some chapter summaries extend the Jordan-crossing portion to Joshua 3:15-17 and the chapter 17 portion to 17:1-5, 11-15; the range given here is the conservative identified text from the Cave 4 catalogue list.
Significance: With 4Q47 it shows that Joshua circulated at Qumran in at least two copies, both fragmentary. Its Jordan-crossing and land-allotment fragments are early witnesses to the text of Joshua, centuries older than the medieval Masoretic codices.

Description: A fragmentary Cave 4 copy of Judges, published by Trebolle Barrera in DJD XIV, preserving parts of Judges 6, the opening of the Gideon story. It is the first of the two Cave 4 Judges copies; the Batch 1 Judges copy is the Cave 1 manuscript 1Q6 (1QJudg).
Significance: Emanuel Tov judged this text manifestly non-aligned, possibly reflecting a different literary edition of Judges, so even its few verses matter for the history of the book's text; it is not simply a duplicate of the Masoretic Text.

Description: A fragmentary Cave 4 copy of Judges, published by Trebolle Barrera in DJD XIV, preserving parts of the closing chapters of Judges: the Levite and his concubine episode (Judges 19) and the aftermath of the war against Benjamin (Judges 21). It is the second Cave 4 Judges copy, distinct from 4Q49.
Significance: One of only three cataloged Qumran copies of Judges (with 1Q6 and 4Q49). Its Judges 21 ending is a very early witness to the book's closing chapters.

Description: Twenty-three fragments from Cave 4, published in DJD XVII (Cross, Parry and Saley), preserving parts of 1 Samuel only: Samuel's farewell, Saul's reign, the anointing of David (1 Samuel 16), David's flight from Saul, and David at Keilah. Shorter catalogue summaries compress this to 1 Samuel 16:1-11; 19:10-17; 20:27-42; 21:1-10; 23:9-17; the fuller range here follows the DJD-based survey of Samuel and Kings.
Significance: Dated to around 250 BCE, it is among the oldest surviving manuscripts of biblical Hebrew and the earliest of the four Qumran Samuel copies, predating the Batch 1 copy 4Q51 (4QSama, 50-25 BCE) by about two centuries.

Description: Three partially preserved columns and four small fragments from Cave 4, published in DJD XVII, preserving the end of David's dealings with Abigail's household (1 Samuel 25) and the Absalom narrative (2 Samuel 14-15). It is the third Cave 4 Samuel copy, distinct from 4Q51 and 4Q52.
Significance: A Hasmonean-period witness to the Absalom revolt narrative, showing Samuel continued to be copied at Qumran in the century before the Batch 1 copy 4Q51 was written.

Description: Nine fragments from Cave 4, seven identified and two unidentified, preserving Solomon's temple furnishings (1 Kings 7: the pillars Jachin and Boaz, the bronze sea and the stands) and the bringing of the ark into the temple (1 Kings 8). One scholarly survey gives the chapter 7 ending as 7:50 rather than 7:51; the range here follows the DSS English Bible edition. It preserves 1 Kings only, unlike the Batch 1 Kings copy 6Q4, which spans 1 and 2 Kings.
Significance: The only Cave 4 copy of Kings and a first-century BCE witness to the temple-building account, complementing the Cave 5 and Cave 6 Kings copies rather than duplicating them.

Description: Three fragments from Cave 5, inscribed in a Hasmonean hand, preserving the opening of 1 Kings: David's old age and the succession struggle in which Bathsheba and Nathan secure Solomon's anointing as king (1 Kings 1). It is the only biblical Kings copy from Cave 5.
Significance: The earliest of the three Qumran Kings copies by date range, and the only one preserving the very beginning of Kings; together with 4Q54 and 6Q4 it gives three independent Qumran witnesses to 1 Kings.

Description: A single small fragment from Qumran Cave 5, published by Milik in DJD III (pp. 173-174) as an Amos manuscript without further comment in the editio princeps. It preserves only the opening oracle against Damascus (Amos 1:2-5). DATE UNCERTAINTY STATED: DJD III dates the script to the 1st century CE; one widely repeated summary gives 50 BC-AD 50, so the entry uses the broader 1st century AD and does not narrow it further. Hartog notes it may have contained only Amos. Its Amos 1:3 reading, mentioning the pregnant women of Gilead, has been cited as Hebrew support for the longer Septuagint reading against the shorter Masoretic Text; other scholars argue the phrase is a contamination from Amos 1:13 — the reading is noted, not settled, here.
Significance: The only Qumran biblical manuscript of the Minor Prophets outside Cave 4, and the only single-book Amos fragment from Qumran: it shows Amos circulating outside the Cave 4 Twelve scrolls, and it is a key witness in the Amos 1:3 text-critical debate (Masoretic Text versus Septuagint).

Description: A fragmentary copy of Daniel from Qumran Cave 1, published as 1Q71. It preserves Daniel 1:10-17 in Hebrew and Daniel 2:2-6 across the book's language switch, Hebrew up to Daniel 2:4a and Aramaic from 2:4b. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's 4QDana (4Q112) and from 1QDanb (1Q72).
Significance: Together with 1QDanb it shows Daniel was read at Qumran in Cave 1 copies as well as Cave 4 copies, and it preserves the exact point where Daniel changes language from Hebrew to Aramaic.

Description: A fragmentary copy of Daniel from Qumran Cave 1, published as 1Q72. It preserves only Daniel 3:22-30, the end of the fiery-furnace story and Nebuchadnezzar's decree, in Aramaic, as in the Masoretic Text's Aramaic section (Daniel 2:4b-7:28). It is a different manuscript from 1QDana (1Q71) and from Batch 1's 4QDana (4Q112).
Significance: A small Aramaic witness to Daniel 3. Its survival in Cave 1, alongside 1QDana, shows the Aramaic stories of Daniel circulated at Qumran independently of the larger Cave 4 copies.

Description: A substantial fragmentary copy of Daniel from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XVI (Ulrich) as 4Q113. Its Aramaic section covers Daniel 5:10-7:28 and its Hebrew section Daniel 8:1-16, spanning the handwriting on the wall, the lions' den, the four beasts and the ram-and-goat vision. The reading at Daniel 7:11 is marked uncertain in the Cave 4 list. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's 4QDana (4Q112). Publish-prep note: Daniel 6:8-22, 27-29 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Daniel 6:7-21, 26-28) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Daniel 5:31 = Hebrew 6:1; English 6:1-28 = Hebrew 6:2-29). The uncertain Daniel 7:11 reading has been removed from PreservedPassages and is stated in the Description.
Significance: The latest-dated Qumran Daniel copy (about AD 20-50). It shows Daniel still being copied in the generation before Qumran's destruction, in both of the book's languages.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Daniel from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XVI (Ulrich) as 4Q114. It preserves only Daniel 10-11, the final vision's opening and the kings of the north and south. Palaeographically it is dated to the late second century BC (Flint's table, citing Ulrich, DJD 16), making it the oldest Qumran Daniel copy; one summary table's 'first half of the second century BC' dating for the next Daniel manuscript (4QDane) is noted there as a presumed typo and is not applied here. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's 4QDana (4Q112).
Significance: The oldest surviving Daniel manuscript. A copy of Daniel 10-11 already existed in the late second century BC, which is central evidence in discussions of when the book of Daniel was composed.

Description: A fragmentary Aramaic copy of Daniel from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XVI (Ulrich) as 4Q115. It preserves passages from Daniel 3 (the furnace), Daniel 4 (Nebuchadnezzar's dream) and Daniel 7 (the beasts and the Ancient of Days), all from the book's Aramaic section. The opening verses at Daniel 3:8-10 are marked uncertain in the Cave 4 list. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's 4QDana (4Q112).
Significance: An Aramaic witness spanning Daniel's court tales and its first apocalyptic vision, showing the Aramaic half of Daniel circulated as a unit at Qumran.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Daniel from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XVI (Ulrich) as 4Q116. It preserves only Daniel 9:12-17, Daniel's prayer of confession over Jerusalem. It is dated elsewhere to the late second century BC; a Flint summary table's 'first half of the second century BC' dating for this manuscript is flagged in that same table as presumably a typo and is not followed here. Because only a single prayer passage survives, the original scope of the scroll cannot be determined from this fragment alone. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's 4QDana (4Q112).
Significance: One of the two oldest Qumran Daniel copies (with 4QDanc). Its single passage is the confession at the heart of Daniel 9, preserved in Hebrew a century and more before the New Testament period.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Daniel on papyrus from Qumran Cave 6, published as 6Q7. It is the only Daniel copy from Cave 6 and the only Qumran Daniel copy on papyrus. It preserves passages from Daniel 8 (Gabriel's interpretation), Daniel 10 (the vision by the Tigris) and Daniel 11 (the wise and the king). One secondary compilation lists Daniel 8:20-21 rather than 8:21-22 for the first passage; the Flint detailed list used here gives 8:16-17, 21-22. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's 4QDana (4Q112).
Significance: The latest material witness in the Daniel group and the papyrus exception: it shows Daniel was still being copied, on a cheaper material, around AD 50, shortly before Qumran's destruction.

Description: A tiny fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q38b, the third fragment grouped as 4QDeutk, preserving only Deuteronomy 30:16-18.
Significance: A single-passage Late Herodian witness to Deuteronomy 30.

Description: A fragment from Qumran Cave 6, catalogued as 6Q20, listed as possibly from Deuteronomy. DISPUTED: the catalogue marks it with a question mark and relates it only tentatively to Deuteronomy 11:10. It is included only with that dispute stated, never as a certain Deuteronomy copy.
Significance: A disputed single-verse fragment; it must not be counted as certain evidence for a Cave 6 Deuteronomy copy.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 11, catalogued as 11Q3, preserving Deuteronomy 1:4-5 and 2:28-30.
Significance: A Late Herodian Cave 11 witness to the opening of Deuteronomy.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 1, catalogued as 1Q4.
Significance: A Cave 1 witness to Deuteronomy across chapters 1-16.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 1, catalogued as 1Q5, with remains spanning most of the book.
Significance: A broad Cave 1 witness to Deuteronomy, from chapter 1 to Moses' blessing in chapter 33.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q10, preserving only Deuteronomy 1:7-9.
Significance: A very small Cave 2 witness to the opening of Deuteronomy.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q11, preserving Deuteronomy 17:12-15 (law of the king).
Significance: A small Cave 2 witness to Deuteronomy 17.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q12, preserving Deuteronomy 10:8-12.
Significance: A small Cave 2 witness to Deuteronomy 10.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q28, among the earliest Deuteronomy copies from Qumran. Publish-prep note: Deuteronomy 23:26-24:8 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Deuteronomy 23:25-24:8) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Deuteronomy 22:30 = Hebrew 23:1; English 23:1-25 = Hebrew 23:2-26).
Significance: One of the oldest Qumran Deuteronomy witnesses, on divorce and related laws.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q29, with remains from the covenant renewal and the Song of Moses.
Significance: An early Hasmonean witness to Deuteronomy 29-32.

Description: A lengthy fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q30, of a textual type related to the Septuagint. Publish-prep note: the compact list notation after cross-chapter ranges has been expanded so the site's passage linker resolves it correctly (same verses claimed, chapters made explicit): '20-17:7, 15-18:1' is now '20-17:7, 17:15-18:1', and '24-28:14, 18-20, 22-25, 29-30, 48-50, 61' is now '27:24-28:14, 28:18-20, 28:22-25, 28:29-30, 28:48-50, 28:61'. Without this, the linker resolved the continuations to chapters 26-27, where verses such as 26:61 do not exist.
Significance: A major Hasmonean witness spanning Deuteronomy 3-32.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q31.
Significance: A Middle Hasmonean witness to Deuteronomy 2-4.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q32.
Significance: A Late Hasmonean witness to Deuteronomy 3, 7 and 8.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q33, with remains across Deuteronomy 4-27. Publish-prep note: Deuteronomy 23:21-26 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Deuteronomy 23:20-25) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Deuteronomy 22:30 = Hebrew 23:1; English 23:1-25 = Hebrew 23:2-26).
Significance: A broad Late Hasmonean witness to Deuteronomy.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q34.
Significance: A Middle Herodian witness to Deuteronomy 9 and 23-28.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q35. Publish-prep note: the compact list '43-2:6, 28-30' has been expanded to '43-2:6, 2:28-30' so the site's passage linker resolves the continuation to chapter 2, the end chapter of the range. Same verses claimed, chapter made explicit.
Significance: A witness to Deuteronomy's opening, its laws, and Moses' blessing.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q36. Publish-prep note: Deuteronomy 23:22-26 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Deuteronomy 23:21-25) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Deuteronomy 22:30 = Hebrew 23:1; English 23:1-25 = Hebrew 23:2-26).
Significance: A Late Hasmonean witness to Deuteronomy laws of warfare and community life.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q38, the first of three fragments grouped as 4QDeutk. Like 4Q41, it belongs to the excerpted-texts group, collecting selected Deuteronomy passages.
Significance: An Early Herodian excerpt witness to Deuteronomy 5, 11 and 32.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q38a, the second fragment grouped as 4QDeutk. Publish-prep note: Deuteronomy 23:22-26 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Deuteronomy 23:21-25) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Deuteronomy 22:30 = Hebrew 23:1; English 23:1-25 = Hebrew 23:2-26).
Significance: An Early Herodian witness to Deuteronomy laws in chapters 19-27.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q39, with remains from the second giving of the tablets through Moses' death.
Significance: A witness to Deuteronomy's covenant curses, renewal, and conclusion.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q40.
Significance: A witness to Deuteronomy 3, 4 and 7.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q42.
Significance: A Late Hasmonean witness to Deuteronomy 2, 4-5, 28 and 29.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q43, preserving the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4-11).
Significance: A small but famous passage: a Late Hasmonean witness to the Shema.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q44, preserving only parts of the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32), and grouped with the excerpted texts.
Significance: A witness to the Song of Moses alone, suggesting excerpted use of Deuteronomy 32.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 5, catalogued as 5Q1.
Significance: An early Cave 5 witness to Deuteronomy 7-9.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Ecclesiastes (Qohelet) from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script. It is the smaller of the two Qumran Ecclesiastes copies: the published count gives it about 21 words against about 125 for 4Q109, preserving only Ecclesiastes 1:10-15, including the saying that there is nothing new under the sun.
Significance: A second, independent early witness to the opening chapter of Ecclesiastes, confirming the book's early circulation alongside the older 4Q109 copy.

Description: An excerpted manuscript from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q37, collecting Deuteronomy passages (Decalogue, Shema, covenant blessings) together with Exodus Passover material, in non-canonical order. NOTE: whether the Exodus and Deuteronomy fragments belong to a single manuscript was long unresolved; a 2023 material reconstruction argues they do, but the transition between the two sets is not preserved, so the unity is stated as argued, not as certain. It appears ONCE here, with both books in Work, and is classified as an excerpt collection rather than a continuous Deuteronomy scroll.
Significance: A late Herodian excerpt collection showing which Deuteronomy and Exodus passages were gathered for liturgical or study use.

Description: A single fragmentary scroll from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q17 (DJD XII), containing the end of Exodus (tabernacle construction) and the beginning of Leviticus. It appears ONCE here, with both books in Work. Dated by some lists to c. 250 BCE, among the earliest Qumran biblical fragments.
Significance: An early witness to the Exodus-Leviticus seam, showing the two books copied in sequence in one scroll.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 1, catalogued as 1Q2, with remains from the wilderness manna account and the giving of the Law.
Significance: A Cave 1 witness to Exodus 16 and 19-21.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q2. Two readings are marked uncertain in the catalogue (Exodus 21:18-20 and 30:21).
Significance: A Cave 2 witness spanning the oppression in Egypt, the plagues, the Passover, and the golden calf episode.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q3. The Exodus 12:26-27 reading is marked uncertain in the catalogue. Publish-prep note: Exodus 21:37-22:2 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Exodus 22:1-3) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Exodus 22:1 = Hebrew 21:37; English 22:2-31 = Hebrew 22:1-30). The uncertain Exodus 12:26-27 reading has been removed from PreservedPassages and is stated in the Description.
Significance: A Cave 2 witness to Exodus laws and covenant material.

Description: A tiny fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q4, preserving only Exodus 5:3-5 (Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh).
Significance: A very small Cave 2 witness to Exodus 5.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q13 (DJD XII), with remains from Exodus 1-5.
Significance: A Herodian-period witness to Israel's oppression, Moses' birth and call.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q14 (DJD XII, 36 fragments), with remains from Exodus 7-18. Publish-prep note: Exodus 7:26-8:1 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Exodus 8:1-5) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Exodus 8:1-4 = Hebrew 7:26-29; English 8:5-32 = Hebrew 8:1-28).
Significance: A substantial Herodian-period witness to the plagues, the Exodus, and the wilderness journey.

Description: A single fragment from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q15, in which Exodus 13:15-16 is followed directly by Exodus 15:1 (the Song of the Sea), suggesting an excerpted or hymnic arrangement rather than a continuous Exodus scroll.
Significance: Notable for its jump from the Passover law to the Song of the Sea; its excerpt character means it must not be cited as a continuous Exodus text.

Description: A single fragment from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q16, preserving Exodus 13:3-5 and 15-16 (Passover observance).
Significance: A small Hasmonean-period witness to Exodus 13.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q18, preserving the crossing of the sea.
Significance: A Hasmonean-period witness to Exodus 14.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q19, preserving Exodus 6:3-6.
Significance: A small Herodian-period witness to God's covenant promise to Moses.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q20, preserving a short plague passage (Hebrew numbering; Exodus 8 in English numbering for part of the range). Publish-prep note: Exodus 7:28-8:2 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Exodus 8:3-6) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Exodus 8:1-4 = Hebrew 7:26-29; English 8:5-32 = Hebrew 8:1-28).
Significance: A very small Herodian-period witness to the plagues.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Exodus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q21, preserving only Exodus 36:9-10 (tabernacle curtains).
Significance: A very small Roman-period witness to Exodus 36.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Ezekiel from Qumran Cave 11, published in DJD XXIII (Herbert) as 11Q4. What could be salvaged from a solid lump was edited by W. H. Brownlee in 1963; only a few words survive from each passage listed above. In orthography and palaeography it is akin to 1QIsab and may be dated at the turn of the era, and it is described as only generally proto-Masoretic, showing distinctive readings alongside agreement with the Masoretic Text. The PreservedPassages above follow the DJD contents list; one secondary compilation instead lists Ezekiel 11:19 in place of 10:11, which is not followed here.
Significance: The only Ezekiel copy from Cave 11 and, with 4QEzeka, one of the two Qumran Ezekiel manuscripts likely to have been a copy of the whole book rather than an excerpt. Its distinctive readings show Ezekiel's text was not yet fully standardized at the turn of the era.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Ezekiel from Qumran Cave 1, published in DJD I (Barthelemy-Milik) as 1Q9. It consists of two fragments, one with letters from three lines that remains unidentified and one preserving legible elements of three lines corresponding to Ezekiel 4:16-5:1, the breaking of the staff of bread in Jerusalem. Its orthography is described as corresponding exactly with the Masoretic Text.
Significance: The only Ezekiel copy from Cave 1 and one of only six Qumran Ezekiel manuscripts in total. Its few legible lines agree exactly with the Masoretic Text, a small early data point for Ezekiel's stability.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Ezekiel from Qumran Cave 3, published in DJD III (Baillet-Milik-de Vaux) as 3Q1. It survives as a small fragment in Herodian script whose identification with Ezekiel 16:31 and 16:33, resting in part on the rare word for a vaulted place, is described as almost certain rather than fully certain; the letters that remain correspond exactly with the orthography of the Masoretic Text. Verse 32 is not counted as preserved.
Significance: The only Ezekiel copy from Cave 3. Its near-certain but not absolute identification is stated here rather than presented as certain, as required for disputed identifications.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Ezekiel from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV as 4Q74. It preserves only the opening vision of the living creatures and the wheels in Ezekiel 1, from the four faces to the expanse over their heads. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's 4QEzeka (4Q73).
Significance: One of only two Qumran copies preserving Ezekiel's inaugural vision (with 11QEzek), it lets the vision's earliest Hebrew wording be checked in two independent copies.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Ezekiel from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV as 4Q75. It preserves only Ezekiel 24:2-3, the opening of the parable of the cauldron on the day Babylon drew close to Jerusalem. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's 4QEzeka (4Q73) and from 4QEzekb (4Q74).
Significance: The smallest Qumran Ezekiel manuscript by content. Its two verses date the cauldron parable's wording to the first century BC, but nothing beyond those verses can be claimed from it.

Description: A single fragmentary scroll from Qumran Cave 4 that originally contained both Genesis and Exodus; only a small Genesis portion (the end of the Flood narrative) survives alongside substantial Exodus material. It appears ONCE here, with both books in Work, and must not be duplicated as a separate Exodus entry. Publish-prep note: the tail ranges (22:14; 27:38-39, 42-43; 34:17-21) were listed without a book label after the Exodus ranges, which made 27:38-39, 42-43 point past the end of Exodus 27 (21 verses); Ulrich's index of biblical passages lists Genesis 27:38-39, 42-43 (with Genesis 22:14 and 34:17-21) as passages of 4QGen-Exod^a, so the book label has been made explicit as Genesis. The chapter range Exodus 1-4 has been expanded to Exodus 1; 2; 3; 4 so each chapter links.
Significance: One of the earliest combined Pentateuch scrolls from Qumran, showing Genesis and Exodus copied in a single scroll in the Hasmonean period.

Description: A single small fragment from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q8a, preserving Genesis 2:17-18. Catalogued separately from 4QGenh (4Q8).
Significance: A tiny witness to the Garden of Eden narrative.

Description: Two very small fragments from Qumran Cave 4, identified by E. Puech as 4QGenn (4Q576). The identification is given as possible remains of Genesis 34 and 50, not as a certain large copy; the fragments are tiny and the reading is tentative.
Significance: A tentative, very small witness to Genesis; included with its uncertainty stated, per the Batch 2 dispute rule.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 1, catalogued as 1Q1.
Significance: An early Cave 1 witness to the Genesis text, preserving scattered passages from the creation, Fall, and patriarchal narratives.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q1.
Significance: A small Cave 2 witness to Genesis, covering part of the Sodom narrative and Esau's genealogy.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q3, preserving parts of the Joseph narrative (Genesis 40-41).
Significance: A Herodian-period witness to the Joseph story in Genesis.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q4, preserving part of the creation account.
Significance: A Hasmonean-period witness to the opening chapters of Genesis.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q6, preserving Jacob's blessing of Joseph's sons.
Significance: A Hasmonean-period witness to Genesis 48.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q7, preserving parts of the creation account.
Significance: A Hasmonean-period witness to the creation narrative.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q8 (4QGenh1). Distinct from 4Q8a, 4Q8b (a paraphrase, excluded) and 4Q8c (a title fragment only, excluded).
Significance: A small Herodian-period witness to the opening of Genesis.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q9, preserving parts of the Joseph narrative.
Significance: A Herodian-period witness to the Joseph story.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q10, preserving parts of the creation and Fall narratives.
Significance: A Herodian-period witness to Genesis 1-3.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q5, with remains from Esau's genealogy, the Joseph narrative, and Jacob's blessing.
Significance: A Herodian-period witness spanning the end of Genesis, including Jacob's final blessing.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Genesis from Qumran Cave 8, catalogued as 8Q1, preserving parts of the Abraham narrative and the Sodom dialogue.
Significance: A Herodian-period Cave 8 witness to Genesis 17-18.

Description: A Greek fragment of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q122 (DJD IX), preserving only Deuteronomy 11:4 (the drowning of Pharaoh's army). Among the earliest Greek biblical fragments from Qumran.
Significance: A tiny but very early Greek witness to Deuteronomy 11.

Description: A Greek papyrus fragment of Exodus from Qumran Cave 7, catalogued as 7Q1, preserving Exodus 28:4-7 (priestly garments). It is a Greek translation, not a Hebrew copy, and is described in some scholarship as closer to the Hebrew text than to the later Septuagint tradition.
Significance: The only identified Greek Exodus fragment from Qumran, attesting Greek Scripture use alongside Hebrew scrolls.

Description: A Greek papyrus manuscript of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q120 (DJD IX), in 97 fragments. It renders the divine name as IAO (a transliteration) rather than translating it as Lord, a feature of early Greek Scripture manuscripts. Publish-prep note: Leviticus 5:16-24 was listed in Septuagint numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Leviticus 5:16-19; 6:1-5) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Leviticus 6:1-7 = Hebrew 5:20-26) and Himbaza's contents table for 4Q120 (5:16-19; 6:1-5 [5:20-24]). The uncertain Leviticus 2:7-8 reading has been removed from PreservedPassages.
Significance: A major Greek witness to Leviticus 1-6, notable for its IAO rendering of the divine name.

Description: A Greek manuscript of Leviticus on leather from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q119 (DJD IX; Rahlfs 801), stored in the Rockefeller Museum, Jerusalem. It is a Greek translation, not a Hebrew copy.
Significance: An early Greek witness to Leviticus 26, attesting the Greek text of the Torah at Qumran.

Description: A Greek manuscript of Numbers from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q121 (DJD IX), whose text shows revision toward the Hebrew Pentateuch. Several readings are marked uncertain in the catalogue.
Significance: A Greek witness to Numbers 3-4, notable for its Hebrew-revision character.

Description: The second Isaiah copy from Qumran Cave 1, also called the Hebrew University Isaiah Scroll. Found in 1947 and purchased by Eleazar Sukenik, it survives darkened and blackened in fragments and in four major sheets carrying the upper section of the last third of the book. Seven fragments of it are also classified as 1Q8. Palaeography dates it to the late Hasmonean or early Herodian period in the first century BC. It is a different manuscript from Batch 1's complete Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa), not a duplicate of it. Publish-prep note: the research listed Isaiah 47:17-49:15 for column VI; Isaiah 47 has only 15 verses in the English KJV and in the Hebrew text, so that range cannot be resolved and is withheld from PreservedPassages pending verification against DJD 32. It is not converted to 48:17 or any other reading; that would be a guess.
ImageCredit: Public domain (Wikimedia Commons, PD-old / Public Domain Mark 1.0)
Significance: The second-most extensive Isaiah witness from Qumran after 1QIsaa: it preserves substantial portions of Isaiah 38-66 alongside scattered earlier passages, so the two Cave 1 copies can be compared against each other and against the Masoretic Text across most of the book.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich). Its surviving verses come from Isaiah 1-23 only; it is not a complete Isaiah scroll.
Significance: One of eighteen fragmentary Isaiah copies from Cave 4. Its verses are a further independent witness to the early Isaiah text, but a fragment of this size proves nothing about passages it does not preserve.

Description: A substantial fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich). Its surviving verses span the whole book, from Isaiah 1 to Isaiah 66, but only in scattered passages; it is not a complete copy.
Significance: One of the two most extensive Cave 4 Isaiah copies (with 4QIsac). Its breadth makes it one of the most useful Cave 4 witnesses for comparing the Qumran Isaiah text with the Masoretic Text across both halves of the book.

Description: A substantial fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich). A distinctive feature noted by Emanuel Tov is that it writes the Tetragrammaton and other divine names in palaeo-Hebrew characters, including prefixes and, uniquely, suffixes of 'elohim in palaeo-Hebrew. Its orthography is close to 1QIsaa in overlapping passages, though the two differ in details.
Significance: The most scribally distinctive Cave 4 Isaiah copy: its palaeo-Hebrew divine names show how a Qumran scribe could mark the divine name as special inside an otherwise ordinary biblical copy, and its overlap with 1QIsaa lets the two copies be compared directly.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich). Its surviving passages come from Isaiah 46-58, including the Servant passage in Isaiah 53:8-12. It is dated to about AD 30-68, the latest of the Qumran Isaiah copies in the BYU summary table.
Significance: Evidence that Isaiah was still being copied at Qumran in the generation before the settlement's destruction in AD 68, not only in the second and first centuries BC.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich). Its surviving passages run from Isaiah 2 to Isaiah 14, with a single later fragment from Isaiah 59:15-16.
Significance: A further early witness to the first half of Isaiah, including the vineyard and throne-vision material of Isaiah 2-14; its scattered survival limits what it can prove beyond those passages.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich). Its surviving passages run from Isaiah 1 to Isaiah 29, including the throne vision in Isaiah 6:3-8, 10-13.
Significance: A Hasmonean-period witness to the opening third of Isaiah. Its readings have been cited in textual studies of Isaiah 6 and 11, but only for the verses it actually preserves.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q61. It preserves only Isaiah 42:14-43:24 in part, from the Servant and exodus-renewal passages. It is a different manuscript from 4QIsah (4Q62), which preserves the preceding verses of Isaiah 42; some secondary lists wrongly give both manuscripts the number 4Q61, and that duplication is not followed here.
Significance: A small but focused witness to Isaiah 42-43, the chapters where the Servant and the new-exodus promises stand side by side; its value is confined to those verses.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q62. It preserves only Isaiah 42:4-11, the opening of the first Servant Song, with a free space at the end of verse 4 marking the passage as a unit of its own. Its DJD number is 4Q62, not 4Q61 as some secondary lists print it; 4Q61 is 4QIsag.
Significance: Though only eight verses survive, they cover the Servant's mission to the coastlands (Isaiah 42:4) and the song of praise that follows, and they confirm the consonantal text of the Masoretic Text there.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q62a. It preserves only part of Isaiah 56:7-57:8, in two fragments, one of which still shows stitching to a previous sheet. A study of its scribal practice describes it as the work of a skilled but hurried scribe, and notes it may have been a bookroll or a series of excerpts rather than a professional full copy; its original scope cannot be determined from what survives.
Significance: A small witness to Isaiah 56-57, including the house-of-prayer passage (Isaiah 56:7). Its scribal features, rather than its length, are what scholars have singled out.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q63. It preserves only the opening six verses of Isaiah, the superscription and the opening accusation against Judah.
Significance: One of several Qumran copies preserving Isaiah's opening chapter, showing that the book's first verses were copied independently in multiple Cave 4 scrolls; it proves nothing beyond Isaiah 1:1-6.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q64. It preserves only the passage spanning the end of Isaiah 28 and the opening of Isaiah 29, the parable of the farmer and the woe over Ariel.
Significance: A narrow witness to Isaiah 28-29. Its value is confined to those verses; it cannot speak for the rest of the book.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q65. It preserves only Isaiah 7:14-15, including the Immanuel sign, and Isaiah 8:11-14.
Significance: A tiny but notable witness: it is one of the Qumran copies preserving Isaiah 7:14, a verse widely cited in Christian tradition, in a Hebrew copy predating the New Testament by a century.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q66. It preserves only the end of Isaiah 60 and the opening of Isaiah 61, including the passage beginning 'The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me'.
Significance: A small witness to Isaiah 60-61, the everlasting-light and good-news passages. Its few verses add one more early Hebrew copy to the evidence for those chapters.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q67. It preserves only Isaiah 58:13-14, the Sabbath-delight passage. Cave 4 lists group it with fragments on punishment and on God's blessings for his people, including 4Q69a.
Significance: A two-verse witness to Isaiah 58. It shows the Sabbath passage circulating at Qumran, but nothing more can be claimed from two verses.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q68. It survives as a single composite fragment preserving Isaiah 14:28-15:2. A 2023 study of its material and scribal features argues it is incompatible with a full copy of the book and may instead derive from a small-scale scroll containing only a subsection of Isaiah, though its precise scope cannot be determined; its variants appear exegetically motivated, clarifying cruxes in its proto-Masoretic Vorlage. It is therefore listed here as a biblical Isaiah fragment, not as a full Isaiah scroll.
Significance: The most recently re-examined small Isaiah fragment: it illustrates how a single fragment can still illuminate scribal interpretation, while warning against assuming every Qumran fragment came from a complete book scroll.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q69a. It preserves only Isaiah 54:10-13, the everlasting-covenant passage ('my steadfast love shall not depart from you').
Significance: A four-verse witness to Isaiah 54. Like the other smallest Cave 4 Isaiah fragments, it adds one more early copy for its verses and nothing beyond them.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q69b. It preserves only a single verse, Isaiah 30:23, on rain for the seed sown in the ground.
Significance: The smallest Qumran Isaiah manuscript by content: a single-verse fragment. It counts as one of the twenty-one Qumran Isaiah copies, but proves nothing beyond Isaiah 30:23.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Skehan-Ulrich) as 4Q69. It is the only Isaiah manuscript from Qumran written on papyrus rather than leather, and it preserves only Isaiah 5:28-30, the closing verses of the Assyrian-invasion passage.
Significance: Its material makes it the exception among Qumran Isaiah copies: a papyrus biblical fragment in a corpus dominated by leather scrolls, showing papyrus was also used for Scripture at Qumran.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Isaiah from Qumran Cave 5, published as 5Q3. It is the only Isaiah copy from Cave 5 and preserves only Isaiah 40:16 and 40:18-19, from the incomparability-of-God passage. It is a different manuscript from the Cave 1 and Cave 4 copies, and from the Wadi Murabba'at Isaiah copy (Mur 3), which is excluded from this batch as a non-Qumran site.
Significance: It completes the Qumran Isaiah count at twenty-one copies (two from Cave 1, eighteen from Cave 4, one from Cave 5), showing Isaiah's exceptional popularity at Qumran despite its tiny surviving content.

Description: The only Jeremiah copy from Qumran Cave 2, published as 2Q13. It preserves parts of Jeremiah 42-49, including the oracles against the nations placed at the end of the book, and is described as semi-Masoretic in text type. Fragments doubtfully identified with this manuscript (Jeremiah 13:22; 32:24-25; 48:2-4, 41-42) are NOT counted in the PreservedPassages above; only the securely identified passages are listed.
Significance: The latest-dated Qumran Jeremiah copy in the group and the only one from Cave 2. Its placement of the oracles against the nations at the end of the book aligns it with the Masoretic order rather than the Septuagint order.

Description: A substantial fragmentary Hebrew copy of Jeremiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Tov) as 4Q70. It is the oldest Jeremiah manuscript from Qumran, dated by Cross to about 225-175 BC, and is proto-Masoretic in text type. Its editor singled it out for its exceptionally high level of secondary scribal activity, including a long insertion by a second scribe in an intercolumn and the bottom margin whose status (correction of a scribal omission versus a genuine textual variant) is debated. Several identifications within it remain uncertain, marked with '?' above, including whether a fragment belongs at Jeremiah 13:22 or 22:3. Publish-prep note: the compact list '28-9:2, 7-15' has been expanded to '28-9:2, 9:7-15' so the site's passage linker resolves the continuation to chapter 9, the end chapter of the range. Same verses claimed, chapter made explicit.
Significance: The earliest surviving Jeremiah copy by more than a century. It shows the proto-Masoretic Jeremiah text already circulating, with heavy scribal correction, in the early second century BC.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Jeremiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV (Tov) as 4Q71. It is a DIFFERENT manuscript from Batch 1's 4QJerc (4Q72) and must not be merged with it: 4QJerb is similar to the Hebrew Vorlage behind the Septuagint, while 4QJerc is semi-Masoretic. In older literature '4QJerb' was also used as an umbrella term covering what are now separately cataloged as 4QJerd (4Q72a) and 4QJere (4Q72b); those are separate entries in this batch. Within Jeremiah 9-10 only scattered verses are securely legible in detail, though the fragments span the range listed above.
Significance: The key Qumran witness to the shorter, Septuagint-type edition of Jeremiah: it proves that two different editions of Jeremiah circulated side by side in the Second Temple period, rather than a single uniform text.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Jeremiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV as 4Q72a, formerly grouped under the umbrella name 4QJerb (olim 4QJerb). It preserves only Jeremiah 43:2-10, from the aftermath of Jerusalem's fall, and is described as partly similar to the Vorlage of the Septuagint. Its dating is given as like that of 4QJerb (4Q71). It is a separate manuscript from both 4QJerb (4Q71) and Batch 1's 4QJerc (4Q72); the similar numbers 4Q72, 4Q72a and 4Q72b must not be conflated.
Significance: A small but textually important fragment: together with 4QJerb it shows the Septuagint-type Jeremiah was represented by more than one Qumran copy, in a passage about the flight to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Jeremiah from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD XV as 4Q72b, formerly grouped under the umbrella name 4QJerb (olim 4QJerb). It preserves only Jeremiah 50:4-6, the opening of the oracle against Babylon, and is described as similar to the Masoretic Text. It is a separate manuscript from 4QJerb (4Q71), 4QJerd (4Q72a) and Batch 1's 4QJerc (4Q72).
Significance: A three-verse Masoretic-type witness to the Babylon oracle, balancing the Septuagint-type fragments from the same book: even within Jeremiah 50, the Qumran evidence is not one-sided.

Description: A single small fragment of a Hebrew copy of Job from Qumran Cave 2, preserving only part of Job 33:28-30. It is the smallest of the six Qumran Job manuscripts (2Q15, 4Q99, 4Q100, 4Q101, 4Q157, 11Q10). No date is stated for it in the published list consulted, so none is given here.
Significance: Its value is narrow but real: even three verses show Job already circulating in Hebrew at Qumran, and its Job 33 text sits alongside the much fuller Job 31-37 witness of 4Q99.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Job from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script. The surviving verses are scattered across Job 8, 9, 13, 14 and 31, so the copy cannot be reconstructed as a continuous run of text.
Significance: An early Hebrew witness to Job's dialogues and to chapter 31, predating the medieval Masoretic manuscripts by about a thousand years; its fragmentary state limits it to confirming, not revising, the early text of those verses.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Lamentations from Qumran Cave 3, dated c. 30 BC-AD 50. It preserves parts of Lamentations 1:10-12 and 3:53-62, the latter only partially.
Significance: With 4Q111, 5Q6 and 5Q7, one of only four Qumran copies of Lamentations, confirming the book's circulation in Hebrew in the 1st century BC-AD.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Lamentations from Qumran Cave 5, dated c. AD 50, preserving parts of Lamentations 4 and 5. It is the second-fullest Qumran Lamentations copy by published word count (about 141 words, against about 193 for 4Q111).
Significance: Preserves the closing chapters of Lamentations, including the prayer of chapter 5, in a 1st-century AD Hebrew copy, complementing 4Q111's opening chapters.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Lamentations from Qumran Cave 5, dated c. 30 BC-AD 50, preserving only Lamentations 4:17-20, the passage about the anointed of the LORD caught in the enemy's pits.
Significance: The smallest Qumran Lamentations copy, but an independent witness to Lamentations 4 alongside the fuller 5Q6 copy from the same cave.

Description: A single fragment from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q26b, preserving Leviticus 7:19-26; it contains the divine name written in paleo-Hebrew script within a square-script text. (No separate 4QLevf is catalogued; the lettering jumps from e to g.)
Significance: A tiny but notable fragment: the paleo-Hebrew divine name inside a square-script Leviticus copy.

Description: A single lengthy scroll from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q23 (DJD XII), containing Leviticus and Numbers in sequence. It appears ONCE here, with both books in Work. Together with 4Q27 (Batch 1), it is one of the two most extensive Numbers scrolls from the Judaean Desert.
Significance: A major Hasmonean-period witness to Leviticus and the first part of Numbers.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 11, catalogued as 11Q2 (DJD XXIII), in nine fragments, seven with Leviticus text; it uses the ancient paleo-Hebrew form for the divine name. Distinct from 11Q1 (Batch 1). Some fragments are dark and unclear, so the passage list follows the published fragment identifications. Publish-prep note: the research listed Leviticus 8:8 or 8:9 for one fragment; the verse is uncertain, so it is not included in PreservedPassages.
Significance: A late Herodian Cave 11 witness to Leviticus, with the paleo-Hebrew divine name.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q24 (DJD XII). NOTE: recent scholarship (Tigchelaar) has argued 4Q24 should be split into two manuscripts (4Q24a, Leviticus 1-3, and 4Q24b, Leviticus 21-25); this entry keeps the traditional single catalogue number, with the split debate stated here, rather than inventing two entries.
Significance: A Hasmonean-period witness to Leviticus offerings, priestly laws, and festivals.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q25, with remains from Leviticus 1, 3-5 and 8. Publish-prep note: the compact list '3:16-4:6, 12-14, 23-28' has been expanded to '3:16-4:6, 4:12-14, 4:23-28' so the site's passage linker resolves the continuations to chapter 4, the end chapter of the range; resolved to chapter 3, verses 3:23-28 do not exist (Leviticus 3 has 17 verses). Same verses claimed, chapters made explicit.
