Significance: A witness to Leviticus offerings and priestly consecration.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q26, in a poor state of preservation, with remains from Leviticus 14, 15 and 17.
Significance: A small witness to Leviticus cleansing and blood laws.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q26a, with remains from Leviticus 2-3 and 19-22. Publish-prep note: the research listed Leviticus 2:11-18, but Leviticus 2 has only 16 verses in the English KJV and in the Hebrew text (SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B lists no versification difference for Leviticus 2), so the range is truncated to 2:11-16 pending verification against DJD. Himbaza's contents table for 4Q26a lists no Leviticus 2 material at all, so the Leviticus 2 fragments should be re-checked by the coordinator. Also, the compact list '27-21:4, 9-12, 21-24' has been expanded to '27-21:4, 21:9-12, 21:21-24' so the linker resolves the continuations to chapter 21, the end chapter of the range, per Himbaza's contents table for 4Q26a (21:1-4, 9-12, 21-24).
Significance: A witness to Leviticus offerings and holiness laws.

Description: A tiny fragmentary Hebrew copy of Numbers from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q8, preserving only Numbers 7:88 (the sum of dedication offerings).
Significance: A single-verse witness to Numbers 7.

Description: A single fragment from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q9, listed as 2QNumd with a question mark. DISPUTED: the fragment may belong to 2Q7 (2QNumb), and it has also been read as Leviticus 23:1-3. It is included only with that dispute stated, never as a certain Numbers copy.
Significance: A disputed single fragment; it must not be counted as certain evidence for a fourth Cave 2 Numbers copy.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Numbers from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q6.
Significance: A Herodian-period witness to the Levite census in Numbers 3-4.

Description: A fragmentary Hebrew copy of Numbers from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q7, preserving part of the wilderness itinerary.
Significance: A small witness to Numbers 33.

Description: A single archaic paleo-Hebrew fragment of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q46, preserving Deuteronomy 26:14-15 (tithes confession). Among the oldest Qumran biblical fragments.
Significance: One of the earliest surviving Deuteronomy fragments, in archaic paleo-Hebrew script.

Description: A paleo-Hebrew manuscript of Deuteronomy from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q45, in 65 fragments, generally agreeing with the Masoretic Text against the Samaritan expansions. Publish-prep note: Deuteronomy 13:19 was listed in Hebrew numbering and has been converted to English KJV numbering (Deuteronomy 13:18) per SBL Handbook of Style Appendix B (English/Hebrew versification table) (English Deuteronomy 12:32 = Hebrew 13:1; English 13:1-18 = Hebrew 13:2-19). Also, the compact list '30-12:1, 11-12' has been expanded to '30-12:1, 12:11-12' so the linker resolves the continuation to chapter 12, the end chapter of the range.
Significance: A major paleo-Hebrew witness to Deuteronomy, spanning chapters 7-34.

Description: A single paleo-Hebrew scroll from Qumran Cave 4, published in DJD IX, containing the end of Genesis (Genesis 50:26) and extensive Exodus material (Exodus 1-36). It appears ONCE here, with both books in Work.
Significance: A major paleo-Hebrew witness to the Pentateuch, showing the old Hebrew script still in use for Torah scrolls in the Hasmonean period.

Description: A single paleo-Hebrew fragment from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q12. DJD IX describes it as a fragment with remains of Genesis 26 only. CORRECTION NOTE: some online lists repeat the long Exodus passage list of 4Q22 (4QpaleoExodm, Batch 1) under 4Q12; that repetition is NOT followed here, because DJD IX assigns 4Q12 only Genesis 26 material.
Significance: A small paleo-Hebrew witness to the Isaac narrative in Genesis 26; its value is limited by its size, and the erroneous Exodus attribution found in some lists must not be repeated.

Description: A paleo-Hebrew fragment of Genesis from Qumran Cave 6, catalogued as 6Q1, preserving God's words to Noah before the Flood.
Significance: An early paleo-Hebrew witness to the Flood narrative.

Description: A fragment of Job from Qumran Cave 4 written in paleo-Hebrew script, the old Hebrew script rather than the square script used by most Qumran biblical copies. It preserves parts of Job 13-14, Job's reply to Zophar and his plea about the brevity of life.
Significance: Shows Job being copied in the archaic script at Qumran alongside square-script copies, and gives an early witness to Job 13-14 independent of the later Masoretic tradition.

Description: A paleo-Hebrew fragment of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 2, catalogued as 2Q5, preserving clean and unclean creatures.
Significance: A small Hasmonean-period paleo-Hebrew witness to Leviticus 11.

Description: A paleo-Hebrew fragment of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 6, catalogued as 6Q2, preserving the anointing of Aaron.
Significance: A very small early paleo-Hebrew witness to Leviticus 8.

Description: A paleo-Hebrew scroll from Qumran Cave 1, catalogued as 1Q3, containing Leviticus material and a Numbers passage. A further fragment with Leviticus 27:30-31 has been tentatively assigned to this manuscript (sometimes labelled 1QpaleoLevb) and is NOT counted as certain here; it is noted only as a possible attribution.
Significance: A Cave 1 paleo-Hebrew witness to Leviticus purity and festival laws, with a Numbers census fragment.

Description: A papyrus fragment from Qumran Cave 6, catalogued as 6Q3, preserving only a few letters of Deuteronomy 26:19.
Significance: A minimal papyrus witness to Deuteronomy 26.

Description: A papyrus fragment from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q483, whose text (Genesis 1:28-29) could belong either to a Genesis copy or to the Book of Jubilees, which retells Genesis. DISPUTED IDENTIFICATION: it is included here only with that dispute stated, never as a certain Genesis copy.
Significance: If Genesis, a small papyrus witness to the creation blessing; if Jubilees, it belongs to that retelling instead — hence the entry must not be cited as proof of a Genesis copy.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew copy of Proverbs from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script. It is the smaller of the two Qumran Proverbs copies: the published statistical count gives it about 42 words against about 126 for 4Q103. It preserves the end of the first wisdom poem (Proverbs 1) and the opening verse of chapter 2.
Significance: An early Hebrew witness to the opening of Proverbs, confirming that the book's first chapters were already circulating in essentially their familiar form in the 1st century BC.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew Psalms copy from Qumran Cave 11, in Herodian script. It is one of the three scrolls (with 11Q5 and 4Q87) attesting the 11QPsalms-type collection, and it also preserves part of the previously unknown Plea for Deliverance also found in 11Q5. Preserved-passage ranges for this manuscript are given in English (KJV) numbering; the manuscript itself carries no modern psalm numbers. Publish-prep note: every PreservedPassages range in this entry was re-versified to English (KJV) numbering against DJD XXIII via Garcia Martinez & Tigchelaar, The Dead Sea Scrolls Study Edition (Hebrew/MT fragment headings), with the SBL Appendix B table. First-pass conversions (over-length ranges only, from the earlier cleanup): Psalms 77:18-21 to 77:17-20. Final pass verified every remaining range as already correct English numbering (untitled psalms and first-clause-title psalms do not shift). The superscriptions of Psalms 78, 133 and 144 stand as the opening clauses of their first verses, which are included in the passage ranges.
Significance: An early Hebrew witness to the Psalms, predating the medieval Masoretic manuscripts by about a thousand years. Its chief value is textual: it shows which psalms and which readings were already in circulation in the Second Temple period, and, where its psalm order differs from the Masoretic Psalter, that the order of the Psalter was not yet fully fixed.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew Psalms copy from Qumran Cave 11, in Herodian script, ranging across Psalms 2-25. Unprovenanced post-2002 fragments sometimes claimed as fragments 3a-b of this manuscript (Psalm 11) are NOT counted here, as they have no Qumran provenance. Preserved-passage ranges for this manuscript are given in English (KJV) numbering; the manuscript itself carries no modern psalm numbers. Publish-prep note: every PreservedPassages range in this entry was re-versified to English (KJV) numbering against DJD XXIII via Garcia Martinez & Tigchelaar, The Dead Sea Scrolls Study Edition (Hebrew/MT fragment headings), with the SBL Appendix B table. First-pass conversions (over-length ranges only, from the earlier cleanup): Psalms 12:5-9 to 12:4-8. Final-pass conversions: Psalms 9:3-7 to 9:2-6; Psalms 18:1-12 to 18:1-11; Psalms 19:4-8 to 19:3-7. All other ranges were verified as already correct English numbering (untitled psalms and first-clause-title psalms do not shift). The superscriptions of Psalms 13, 14 and 18 are also preserved; the passage ranges give body verses only (the Psalm 14 superscription stands as the opening clause of verse 1).
Significance: An early Hebrew witness to the Psalms, predating the medieval Masoretic manuscripts by about a thousand years. Its chief value is textual: it shows which psalms and which readings were already in circulation in the Second Temple period, and, where its psalm order differs from the Masoretic Psalter, that the order of the Psalter was not yet fully fixed.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew Psalms copy from Qumran Cave 11, in Herodian script, ranging across Psalms 6-116. Preserved-passage ranges for this manuscript are given in English (KJV) numbering; the manuscript itself carries no modern psalm numbers. Publish-prep note: every PreservedPassages range in this entry was re-versified to English (KJV) numbering against DJD XXIII via Garcia Martinez & Tigchelaar, The Dead Sea Scrolls Study Edition (Hebrew/MT fragment headings), with the SBL Appendix B table. First-pass conversions (over-length ranges only, from the earlier cleanup): Psalms 36:13 to 36:12; 39:13-14 to 39:12-13. The superscriptions of Psalms 37, 40 and 68 are also preserved; the passage ranges give body verses only (the Psalm 37 superscription stands as the opening clause of verse 1).
Significance: An early Hebrew witness to the Psalms, predating the medieval Masoretic manuscripts by about a thousand years. Its chief value is textual: it shows which psalms and which readings were already in circulation in the Second Temple period, and, where its psalm order differs from the Masoretic Psalter, that the order of the Psalter was not yet fully fixed.

Description: A single small fragment from Qumran Cave 11, catalogued as 11QPse with a question mark in some editions and described as 'possibly' a Psalms copy in the Cave 11 survey. It preserves only Psalm 50:3-7. It is included here ONLY with that uncertainty stated: its status as a separate Psalms manuscript is not certain. Preserved-passage ranges for this manuscript are given in English (KJV) numbering; the manuscript itself carries no modern psalm numbers.
Significance: An early Hebrew witness to the Psalms, predating the medieval Masoretic manuscripts by about a thousand years. Its chief value is textual: it shows which psalms and which readings were already in circulation in the Second Temple period, and, where its psalm order differs from the Masoretic Psalter, that the order of the Psalter was not yet fully fixed.

Description: Fragments of a Hebrew Psalms copy from Qumran Cave 1, arranged stichometrically (verse lines), with the divine name written in palaeo-Hebrew characters. Further fragments of the same manuscript remain unidentified. Preserved-passage ranges for this manuscript are given in English (KJV) numbering; the manuscript itself carries no modern psalm numbers. Description: A tiny fragment of a Hebrew copy of the Song of Solomon from Qumran Cave 4, containing only ten letters from two lines: five letters from Song 3:7 (the end of 'Solomon' and 'sixty') and one word from Song 3:8 ('equipped'). Description: Fragments of an Aramaic Targum (translation) of Job from Qumran Cave 4, in Herodian script. This is a translation of Job, not a Hebrew copy: it renders Job 3 and Job 4-5 into Aramaic, and it is the smaller of the two Qumran Job targums (the other is 11Q10).
Significance: Evidence that Job was not only copied in Hebrew at Qumran but also translated into Aramaic for hearers or readers who needed it, centuries before the later rabbinic targums; as a translation it witnesses to interpretation of Job, not directly to the Hebrew wording.

DateApprox: c. first half of 1st century AD
Description: A substantial Aramaic Targum (translation) of Job from Qumran Cave 11, preserved in 39 columns but incompletely, covering Job 17:14 to 42:11 with gaps. It is written in late Herodian script, dated by Zuckerman to c. the first half of the 1st century AD. Some scholars label it more neutrally as an Aramaic version of Job rather than a targum in the later rabbinic sense, since its translation technique (including deliberate omission and re-reading in difficult passages) differs from later targums; that debate is stated, not settled, here.
Significance: The fullest ancient Aramaic witness to Job and the clearest proof that Job was studied in Aramaic at Qumran. Its differences from the Hebrew text show how Job was understood and explained in the 1st century AD, while its gaps mean it cannot be quoted as a complete Aramaic Job.

Description: An Aramaic translation (targum) of Leviticus from Qumran Cave 4, catalogued as 4Q156, preserving parts of Leviticus 16 (Day of Atonement). It is a translation, not a Hebrew copy, and is included as such, with that distinction stated.
Significance: The Qumran Aramaic witness to Leviticus 16, showing the Torah also circulated in Aramaic translation.

Description: A single fragment from the beginning of a Twelve Prophets roll, surviving only with Hosea material (Hosea 1:6-2:5 in the standard summary; Sinclair's first publication is titled for Hosea 1:7-2:5). Whether the original roll contained the whole Twelve is unknown: Hartog notes the remaining fragments contain only Hosea and the manuscript may well have had only part of the Twelve, perhaps even just Hosea, while Brooke suggested it is quite possible it contained the whole Twelve with Hosea at the start; that wider claim is not counted here. DJD XV (Fuller) is the edition of record.
Significance: The earliest surviving Hosea material at Qumran outside the larger Twelve scrolls, preserving the opening of Hosea (the naming of Hosea's children and the opening of the marriage accusation in chapter 2). It is evidence that the Twelve could be copied in smaller sets or as a single-book excerpt as well as in full Twelve scrolls, rather than always as one fixed twelve-book collection.

Description: Two small fragments of a Twelve Prophets manuscript: one Jonah fragment (the storm, the casting of lots, and Jonah thrown into the sea, Jonah 1:6-8, 10-16) and one Micah fragment. UNCERTAIN IDENTIFICATION, STATED NOT HIDDEN: the Micah material (Micah 5:1-2, English numbering; Hebrew 4:14-5:1, so the Bethlehem ruler verse is English Micah 5:2) rests on fragment 5 of this manuscript, and Hartog reports that it is not certain that fragment 5 really belongs to 4Q81 (Garcia Martinez criticised Fuller's joining of fragment 5). The Micah passage is therefore carried with a question mark and must not be cited as a certain Micah witness without that caveat. The manuscript was first published as a separate Micah fragment (Fuller, RevQ 1993) before being joined to the Twelve manuscript in DJD XV.
Significance: A second, independent Qumran witness to Jonah 1 beyond the large Twelve scrolls, and — if fragment 5 belongs — the only Qumran witness to the Bethlehem ruler passage (Micah 5:2) outside the larger scrolls. Its value for Micah depends entirely on the disputed fragment join, which is why the Micah attribution is flagged uncertain here.
